en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Almsfood, 31.
The Training Rule on Lodging Almsfood.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, not far from Sāvatthī, a meal-offering had been prepared for a certain association.
In the morning, the group-of-six bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms; failing to receive any alms, they went to that dwelling.
People, thinking, “The venerable ones have come after such a long time,” served them with great care.

Then on the second day as well... and on the third day as well, the group-of-six monks dressed in the morning, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Not receiving any alms, they went to a lodging and ate there.
Then it occurred to the group-of-six monks:
“What shall we do by going to the monastery?
We will have to come back here again tomorrow,” they said;
and so, staying right there night after night, they ate the alms-food provided at the guest-house.
The sectarians departed.
People criticized, complained, and grumbled, saying:
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, stay again and again and eat alms-food from a guest-house?"
"It is not only for these people that the alms-food of the guesthouse has been prepared; it has been prepared for all.
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six monks, having stayed repeatedly, eat alms-food from a rest-house? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you, having stayed repeatedly, eat alms-food from a rest-house?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, having stayed [there] again and again, eat alms-food from a guest-house?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘One may eat a single meal at a public rest-house. Should one eat more than that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, while the Venerable Sāriputta was traveling through the Kosalan country on his way to Sāvatthī, he approached a certain guesthouse.
Thinking, “The Elder has come after a long time,” the people served him with great care.
Then, after the Venerable Sāriputta had finished eating, a severe illness arose, and he was unable to depart from that lodging.
Then those people said to the Venerable Sāriputta on the second day as well:
"Eat, venerable sir."
Then the Venerable Sāriputta,
being scrupulous because "the Blessed One has prohibited repeatedly staying at a lodging and eating the alms-food of that lodging," did not accept it;
thus he missed his meal.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow, monks, a sick monk to eat the alms-food of a lodging-house after staying there repeatedly.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
‘A monk who is not sick may eat one meal at a lodging-house. Should he eat more than that, it is an offense entailing expiation.’”
"Not ill" means he is able to depart from that lodging.
"Ill" means...
He was unable to depart from that lodging.
What is called "lodging-food" is any one of the five kinds of cooked food prepared for as much as is needed, without distinction, in a hall, a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or in the open air.
A monk who is not ill may eat once. If he receives food with the intention of eating more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is not ill perceives himself as not ill and eats more than one meal at a public alms-feast, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is not ill, being doubtful, eats more than that [allowance] of alms-food from a lodging, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is not ill, perceiving himself as ill, eats more than that [allowance] of alms-food from a lodging, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is ill, perceiving himself as not ill, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If one who is ill is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one who is ill perceives oneself as being ill, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If one who is not ill eats once for the sake of one who is ill;
or if one eats while going or while returning.
The owners, having invited them, feed them;
it is prepared specifically for them,
not prepared as much as they require.
Except for the five kinds of food, there is no offense in all other cases;
nor is there an offense for one who is insane or for a first-time offender.
The training rule on alms-food from a guest-house is finished; this is the first.
